corrected_value.title: Power and relationship commitment: Their impact on marketing channel member performance.

decisions.location: Section 5.3 (The comparison of the results in the United States and those of Brown et al. (1995)), lines 1252-1274; References, lines 1447-1449
decisions.quote:
We find that the impact of non-mediated power  on normative relationship commitment and 

that  of  mediated  power  on  instrumental  relationship  commitment  in  the  United  States  are 

consistent with the findings of Brown et al. (1995). Moreover, the results show that expert and 

legitimate power are negatively associated with whereas referent power is positively associated 

with  instrumental  relationship  commitment,  which  provides  a  possible  explanation  of  the 

finding  of  the  insignificant  effect  of  non-mediated  power  on  instrumental  relationship 

commitment  (Brown  et  al.,  1995).  The  result  reveals  that  different  bases  of  non-mediated 

power  may  have  conflicting  effects  on  instrumental  relationship  commitment  and  hence 

researchers need to consider the individual effects of different bases of non-mediated power. 

Moreover, we find that reward, coercive and legal legitimate power do not significantly affect 

normative relationship  commitment,  whereas Brown et  al. (1995) find that mediated power 

significantly reduces normative relationship commitment.
decisions.reason: 1. Empirical retesting: Zhang, Zhao, Huo, & Flynn (2022) collect new survey data from United States manufacturers (N = 202) to test the power-relationship commitment hypotheses originally tested in the United States by Brown, Lusch, & Nicholson (1995) (Introduction, lines 115-129, 207-210) and dedicate Section 5.3 (lines 1250-1286) to directly comparing their US empirical findings against Brown et al.'s (1995) findings on mediated/non-mediated power, instrumental/normative commitment, and power-symmetry moderation. Consistent with the Coleman pilot objection, explicit empirical retesting and results comparison in a dedicated results/discussion subsection establishes a genuine replication target rather than mere background. 2. Report equivalence does not apply. 4. Prior adjudication: Neither prior_adjudication_path nor prior_state_path exists for this work.

decisions.location: Experiment 3 introduction and Method, lines 273-277; Discussion Experiment 3 and General Discussion, lines 303-309, 355-383; References, line 428
decisions.quote:
Considering that Mechanical Turk workers from the United States are experienced, and that the intuitive-cooperation effect interacts with experience, it might be possible that Rand and colleagues
[8]
recent failures to find an intuitive-cooperation effect in Mechanical Turk experiments as well as our failures to find such an effect in Experiment 1 and in Experiments 2a, 2b and 2c are due to the Mechanical Turk population becoming increasingly experienced in playing public good games. In order to test this experience hypothesis of our replication failures, we conducted a third experiment.
Method
Experiment 3 was an exact replication of our Experiment 2c, but we only tested naïve participants.
decisions.reason: 1. Empirical retesting: After Experiments 1 and 2a-2c fail to replicate the baseline intuitive-cooperation effect of Rand, Greene, & Nowak (2012) [1] Study 6, Verkoeijen & Bouwmeester (2014) note (lines 260-271, 355-363) that Rand et al. (2014) [8] documented a decline of the intuitive-cooperation effect among experienced Mechanical Turk workers and conceptually replicated the interaction with experience showing that the intuitive-cooperation effect holds among naïve participants. Verkoeijen & Bouwmeester (2014) then conduct Experiment 3 with naïve Mechanical Turk participants specifically to empirically test this experience hypothesis and compare their naïve-participant results against Rand et al. [1], [8] (lines 273-279, 303-309, 377-383). Under the codebook replication-chain rule, Rand et al. (2014) [8] is directly retested in Experiment 3. 2. Source-backed identity: Reference 8 (line 428) identifies 'Rand DG, Peysakhovich A, Kraft-Todd GT, Newman GE, Wurzbacher O, et al. (2014) Social heuristics shape intuitive cooperation. Nat. Commun. In press.' (no DOI printed in the primary source). 3. Absence and non-equivalence: The sole shipped row (input_row_index 1122, 10.1038/nature11467) is Rand, Greene, & Nowak (2012) in Nature (represented by sibling target_index 0). Rand et al. (2014) is a separate seven-author Nature Communications article reporting new empirical studies and Mechanical Turk decline data, not an alternate report of the 2012 Nature paper. 4. decisions.quote: In Logemann et al (1978; 1981) two speech pathology/ phonetician experts evaluated 200 PwP showing a range of overall motor and speech severities. It is unclear in the 1978 study how many of the 200 actually entered the analyses for articulation, but from the 1981 study it appears clear it was only 90. Participants read eleven sentences. Each sentence elicited words focused on a different place and manner of consonant articulation (e.g. bilabial plosives; alveolar fricatives; palatal-alveolar affricates), aiming to cover all phonemes of English across a variety of syllable and word positions. The 1978 study reported outcomes according to whether a target sound was heard by the speech pathologists as misarticulated or not; the 1981 study examined the same data employing phonetic transcription.
decisions.reason: 1. Report equivalence with shipped row 2332: Read, Miller, & Kitsou (2018) test a single shared claim—that there is a posterior-to-anterior order of loss of speech sound accuracy in Parkinson's disease—jointly attributed to the linked reports of Logemann, Fisher, Boshes, & Blonsky (1978) (retained in shipped input_row_index 2332, 10.1044/jshd.4301.47, and matched by sibling target_index 0) and Logemann & Fisher (1981) (candidate target_index 1). 2. Positive primary-source evidence of shared underlying study/data: The primary text explicitly states on page 3 (and reiterates on page 19) that Logemann et al. (1978) and Logemann & Fisher (1981) are a 'pair of studies... in linked perceptual studies' in which the same two experts evaluated the exact same 200 PwP dataset reading the same 11 sentences ('The 1978 study reported outcomes according to whether a target sound was heard by the speech pathologists as misarticulated or not; the 1981 study examined the same data employing phonetic transcription'). Even the blind coder noted in coding reasoning that 'their original data were shared'. 3. Conclusion: Consistent with the pilot objections on multi-report studies of one underlying experiment/dataset (such as Ebbinghaus 1880/1885 and ENIGMA 2018/2021), Logemann & Fisher (1981) is a companion report of the same original study and finding already represented by shipped input_row_index 2332 (and sibling target_index 0), not an independent missing original study. 4. Prior adjudication: Neither prior_adjudication_path nor prior_state_path exists for this work.

decisions.quote: Specifically, Eagle et. al. (1966) found that semantic access was granted for a silhouette of a duck on the groundside of a tree image. The result of which caused more duck-related imagery within participants drawing than in participants who viewed just a tree image. The goal of the following study is to replicate the crucial findings of Eagle et. al. (1966). Three experiments were conducted attempting to replicate the original findings but were unable to do so.

corrected_value.title: Tracking lexical consolidation with ERPs: Lexical and semantic-priming effects on N400 and LPC responses to newly-learned words.

decisions.location: Introduction (The Current Study), lines 216-228; see also lines 168-183, Discussion lines 777-812, and References lines 995-998
decisions.quote:
Bakker et al. (2015) findings may thus be
unique for multilingual participants with extensive experience learning for-
eign languages, and may not generalize to all learners, including learners with
little foreign language learning experience. This question was addressed in
the present study by testing learners who have little experience with learning
foreign languages and who are functionally monolingual.
     Taken together, the current study sought to conceptually replicate and extend
the findings of Bakker et al. (2015), and investigate novel vocabulary learn-
ing in monolingual English speakers with minimal foreign language learning
experience. In addition, we examined whether an extended period of offline
consolidation would further enhance semantic integration by testing learners
immediately after learning and one day after learning, as well as one week after
learning.
decisions.reason: 1. Empirical retesting: Liu & van Hell (2020) explicitly state that their ERP study 'sought to conceptually replicate and extend the findings of Bakker et al. (2015)' (lines 222-223), retesting whether newly learned words Paired with novel definitions elicit N400 and LPC lexical (old/new) and semantic-priming ERP effects immediately and 24 hours after training (as well as 1 week later) in monolingual English learners, and directly comparing their N400 and LPC ERP findings to Bakker et al. (2015) throughout the Results and Discussion (lines 715-720, 777-812, 855-866). 2. Source-backed identity: The reference list (lines 995-998) cites only one 2015 work by Bakker et al.: 'Bakker, I., Takashima, A., vanHell, J. G., Janzen, G., & McQueen, J. M. (2015). Tracking lexical consolidation with ERPs: Lexical and semantic-priming effects on N400 and LPC responses to newly-learned words. Neuropsychologia, 79, 33–41. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2015.10.020'. 3. Absence and non-equivalence against shipped row 845: Luna triage erred in claiming that the reference list matches shipped input_row_index 845. Shipped row 845 has doi_o '10.1162/jocn_a_00801' and title_o 'Changes in Theta and Beta Oscillations as Signatures of Novel Word Consolidation' (Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 2015, 27(7), 1286-1297). That shipped JOCN paper is not cited anywhere in Liu & van Hell (2020) and investigates theta and beta time-frequency oscillatory power rather than the N400 and LPC event-related potential (ERP) semantic-priming and old/new effects retested by Liu & van Hell (2020). Thus the actual replicated ERP paper and finding (10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2015.10.020) is absent from the shipped rows. 4.
